fault: Racket preparation begins late, so the shuttle is met behind the body and the clear falls short.
corrections: The racket is prepared late on the backhand side, so the shuttle is met behind the body and the clear falls short. Start the backswing as the opponent makes contact, not as the shuttle crosses the net.
Racket preparation is too slow on the backhand, meeting the shuttle behind the body and losing depth on the clear. Begin the backswing earlier, on the opponent's contact.
The backswing starts too late, so contact happens behind the head and the shot has no length. Get the racket up as soon as the opponent strikes.

fault: The smash is hit with the arm alone and little body rotation, producing pace but no steep angle.
corrections: The smash is hit flat with the arm alone and little body rotation, so it carries pace but no steep angle. Rotate the hips and shoulders through the shot and make contact further in front and higher.
There is no trunk rotation into the smash, producing a flat trajectory that is easy to defend. Turn the body through the shot and take the shuttle higher and earlier.
The smash comes from the arm rather than the body, so it lacks downward angle. Drive the hip and shoulder through and meet the shuttle in front of the head.

fault: The player stays forward after a net shot instead of recovering, leaving the rear court open.
corrections: Recovery to the base position is incomplete after the net shot, leaving the rear court open. Push off the lunge immediately and take two recovery steps back towards centre.
After the net shot the player stays forward instead of recovering, exposing the rear court. Drive off the front foot and move back to base straight away.
There is no recovery after playing at the net, so the back of the court is undefended. Push back off the lunging leg and reset to base before the opponent hits.

fault: The split step lands after the opponent has struck the shuttle, delaying the first movement.
corrections: The split step is late, landing after the opponent has already struck the shuttle, which delays the first movement to the corners. Time the split to land just before their contact.
Split-step timing is late relative to the opponent's contact, costing a step towards the corner. Land the split just as they begin their forward swing.
The split lands too late to help, so the first step is slow. Aim to be landing from the split at the moment the opponent hits.

fault: The low serve is struck from too low and too far back, letting the receiver attack it.
corrections: The serve is struck from too low and too far behind the front service line, giving the receiver time to attack it. Contact the shuttle higher and stand closer to the line to flatten the trajectory.
The low serve is released from below the ideal contact point and lands short, letting the receiver step in and kill it. Take the contact higher and closer to the service line.
Serving from too deep and too low makes the shuttle rise, which invites the attack. Move up to the line and push the shuttle flat across the tape.

fault: The defensive block is played with a tense grip and square racket face, so it sits up mid-court.
corrections: Defence is played with a flat racket face and a stiff wrist, so blocks pop up mid-court. Relax the grip and angle the face slightly downward to drop the block tighter to the net.
The defensive block sits up because the grip is tense and the face is square. Loosen the grip on contact and tilt the racket face down to keep the block low.
A tight grip is sending the block high into the mid-court. Soften the fingers at contact and angle the face down so the shuttle falls short of the service line.

fault: The player side-shuffles into the rear forehand corner instead of scissoring, arriving late and having to lift.
corrections: Footwork into the forehand rear corner uses a side shuffle rather than a scissor jump, arriving late and forcing a defensive lift. Use a scissor-kick take-off so the shuttle can be met in front and attacked.
The player shuffles into the rear forehand corner instead of scissoring, arriving behind the shuttle and having to lift. Adopt a scissor jump to attack from the back.
Shuffling to the rear forehand means arriving under the shuttle rather than behind it. Use a scissor jump so the shuttle can be taken in front and hit down.

fault: The same shot is repeated from the same position, letting the opponent anticipate and move early.
corrections: Shot selection is predictable: three consecutive cross-court clears from the same position let the opponent anticipate and move early. Mix straight drops and half smashes from the same preparation.
The player repeats the cross-court clear from an identical setup, so the opponent reads it and starts moving early. Vary the shot from the same preparation to disguise the intention.
Repeating one shot from one position makes the play readable. Play a different shot from the same preparation so the opponent has to wait.

fault: The player reaches for the net shot without lunging, arriving off balance and unable to recover.
corrections: The net shot is played by reaching rather than lunging, so the player is off balance and cannot recover. Step through into a lunge with the racket leg and keep the head up over the front knee.
Reaching at the net instead of lunging leaves the player stretched and slow to reset. Take a proper lunge onto the racket foot so the push back to base is available.
There is no lunge into the net shot, so balance and recovery are both lost. Drive the racket leg forward into the lunge and push straight back off it.

fault: The clear is hit with the arm alone and lands short, giving the opponent an attacking position.
corrections: The clear is played with the arm alone and lands short of the rear court, handing the opponent an attack. Turn the shoulders into the shot and contact the shuttle higher and further in front.
There is no shoulder rotation in the clear, so it lacks length and drops mid-court. Rotate the upper body through the shot and take the shuttle at full stretch.
The clear falls short because the power comes only from the forearm. Use the shoulder turn and hit the shuttle high and in front to get the length.

fault: The shuttle is allowed to fall below the tape before contact at the net, forcing a lift.
corrections: The shuttle is allowed to drop below the net tape before contact, so the only option left is a lift. Move earlier and take the shuttle at or above tape height to keep the attacking options.
Contact at the net happens below net height, which removes every attacking choice. Get to the shuttle sooner and meet it level with the tape.
Waiting for the shuttle to fall below the net forces a defensive lift. Move in earlier so the shuttle can be met high and tumbled or killed.

fault: The drop shot is telegraphed by a visibly slower swing, so the opponent starts forward early.
corrections: The drop shot is given away by a slower arm speed than the clear, so the opponent moves forward early. Keep the swing speed identical and slow the racket only at contact.
A visibly softer swing telegraphs the drop, letting the opponent read it from the preparation. Match the swing to the clear and take the pace off at the last moment.
The opponent reads the drop because the preparation changes. Keep the same fast preparation and only decelerate the racket head into contact.

fault: The grip is not changed for the backhand, weakening the shot and limiting reach.
corrections: The forehand grip is retained on the backhand side, which weakens the shot and limits reach. Rotate to a backhand grip with the thumb along the flat bevel as the racket comes up.
There is no grip change into the backhand, so the contact is weak and the reach is short. Turn the hand to place the thumb on the wide bevel before contact.
Playing the backhand with a forehand grip loses power and control. Change the grip on the way up so the thumb sits behind the handle at contact.

fault: The landing after the jump smash is off balance, so the recovery to base is slow.
corrections: The landing after the smash is off balance, so the recovery to base is slow and the follow-up is missed. Land on the racket foot with the body facing forward and push straight into the recovery step.
Balance is lost on landing after the jump smash, delaying the move back to base. Land in a controlled scissor and drive the first recovery step immediately.
An unbalanced landing costs the follow-up attack. Land facing the net with weight over the racket foot and push straight back towards centre.

fault: The defensive lift is played flat and short, handing the opponent an easy attack.
corrections: Under pressure the lift is played flat and lands mid-court, giving the opponent a free attack. Get under the shuttle and lift high to the back tramlines to buy recovery time.
The defensive lift is too flat and too short, so the attack continues immediately. Lift steeply and deep to the rear court to reset the rally.
A flat lift keeps the opponent attacking. Take the shuttle earlier, get the racket underneath it and send it high and deep.

fault: The base position is too far forward, leaving the rear court exposed to the clear.
corrections: The base position is too far forward, so any clear to the rear court wins the rally outright. Recover to a base just behind the centre of the court, level with the front service line's midpoint.
Standing too close to the net as a base leaves the back court open. Reset slightly behind centre so both corners are reachable in two steps.
The recovery position is too far up the court, so the deep clear is unreachable. Take base a little further back so the rear corners stay covered.
